ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the circuit diagram there is an operational amplifier, the output terminal is labeled e_o, and is measured by an ideal voltmeter. The output terminal is fed back through a 1 MΩ resistor to the inverting input terminal. The non-inverting input terminal is grounded through another 1 MΩ resistor. The two resistor values are equal, both being 1 MΩ. Reasoning: Denote the bias currents of the two input terminals of the op amp respectively as I_B+ and I_B−, and assume that due to the effect of negative feedback, the inverting terminal and the non-inverting terminal satisfy the virtual short condition, namely V− = V+. The non-inverting terminal is grounded through a 1 MΩ resistor, so the voltage of this node is produced by I_B+ on this resistor. The inverting terminal is connected to the output e_o through a 1 MΩ feedback resistor, so the voltage of this node is determined by the feedback resistor relationship between I_B− and the output. Since the two resistors are equal, after writing the KCL of the two input nodes, one can obtain e_o = 1 MΩ × (I_B− − I_B+) (the sign depends on the current direction convention). Therefore the measured e_o can only give the difference between the two input bias currents, namely the input offset current, and cannot separately find the two bias currents or the average input bias current.

method.method_draft: Model the op-amp inputs as drawing bias currents I_B+ and I_B−. Write KCL at the non-inverting input through its 1 MΩ resistor to ground and at the inverting input through the 1 MΩ feedback resistor from e_o. Apply the virtual-short condition from negative feedback. The equal resistor values make the output voltage equal to 1 MΩ times the difference of the two input bias currents, so the measured e_o allows calculation of the input offset current only.
